limt↓01t​(OTε​(μt,νt)−OTε​(μ,ν))=γ1​φ1(μ,ν)+γ2​φ0(μ,ν).\lim_{t\downarrow 0}\frac{1}{t}\left(\text{OT}_{\varepsilon}\left(\mu_{t},\,\nu_{t}\right)-\text{OT}_{\varepsilon}\left(\mu,\,\nu\right)\right)=\gamma^{1}\varphi_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)}+\gamma^{2}\varphi_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)}.

∎

Now we focus on the first-order Hadamard differentiability of the function (μ,ν)↦(φ1(μ,ν),φ0(μ,ν)),𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→ℋ×ℋ(\mu,\nu)\mapsto(\varphi_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)},\varphi_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)}),\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H}.

Lemma C.5 (Hadamard differentiability of entropic potentials in 𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})).

The 𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)→𝒞​(𝒴)×𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\to\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}) map (μ,ν)↦(φ1(μ,ν),φ0(μ,ν))(\mu,\nu)\mapsto(\varphi_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)},\varphi_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)}) is Hadamard differentiable at (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu), tangentially to ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu}.

Proof.

The Hadamard differentiable of the map Φ:(μ,ν)↦(φ1(μ,ν),φ0(μ,ν))\Phi:(\mu,\nu)\mapsto(\varphi_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)},\varphi_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)}) in 𝒞​(𝒴)×𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}) has been established in the dual Hölder space topology by Goldfeld et al. (2024, Thm. 3), and in the Gaussian RKHS topology by Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Cor. 43), with the latter deriving explicit derivatives. Extending the differentiability in the Sobolev RKHS topology for measures follows by continuously embedding the Gaussian RKHS in the Sobolev RKHS. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be the Gaussian RKHS with kernel (y1,y2)↦exp⁡(−‖y1−y2‖2/2​ε)(y_{1},y_{2})\mapsto\exp(-\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|^{2}/2\varepsilon), with norm ∥⋅∥𝒢\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal{G}} and unit ball denoted by 𝒢1\mathcal{G}_{1}. The Hadamard differentiability of Φ\Phi as a map 𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(𝒢1)×ℓ∞​(𝒢1)→𝒞​(𝒴)×𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1})\to\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}), is established in Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Cor. 43). We show that the same map is Hadamard differentiable when the domain is instead equipped with the stronger topology induced by ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}).

By the continuous embedding of the Gaussian RKHS into the Sobolev RKHS, there exists a constant Cs>0C_{s}>0 such that for any g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, ‖g‖ℋ≤Cs​‖g‖𝒢\|g\|_{\mathcal{H}}\leq C_{s}\|g\|_{\mathcal{G}}. Now we dualize this inclusion. If g∈𝒢1g\in\mathcal{G}_{1}, then Cs−1​g∈ℋ1C_{s}^{-1}g\in\mathcal{H}_{1}. Therefore, for every signed measure γ\gamma,

‖γ‖ℓ∞​(𝒢1)=supg∈𝒢1|∫g​𝑑γ|≤Cs​suph∈ℋ1|∫h​𝑑γ|=Cs​‖γ‖ℓ∞​(ℋ1).\left\|\gamma\right\|_{\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1})}=\sup_{g\in\mathcal{G}_{1}}\left|\int g\,d\gamma\right|\leq C_{s}\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{1}}\left|\int h\,d\gamma\right|=C_{s}\left\|\gamma\right\|_{\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})}.

Therefore, the identity map from ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→ℓ∞​(𝒢1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1}) is continuous. Since Φ\Phi is Hadamard differentiable at (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) as a map defined on 𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(𝒢1)×ℓ∞​(𝒢1)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1}), the defining limit remains valid for any perturbation sequences converging in the stronger topology ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}). So the Hadamard expansion proved in Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Cor. 43) applies without change.

Therefore, Φ\Phi as a map 𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→𝒞​(𝒴)×𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}), is Hadamard differentiable at (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu) tangentially to ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu}. Moreover, the Hadamard derivative is exactly the same as the derivative obtained when the domain is viewed as a subset of ℓ∞​(𝒢1)×ℓ∞​(𝒢1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{G}_{1}). ∎

Now, we lift the Hadamard differentiability of entropic potentials from 𝒞​(𝒴)×𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}) to ℋ×ℋ\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H}.

Proposition C.6 (Hadamard differentiability of entropic potentials in ℋ\mathcal{H}).

The 𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)→ℋ×ℋ\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\to\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} map (μ,ν)↦(φ1(μ,ν),φ0(μ,ν))(\mu,\nu)\mapsto(\varphi_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)},\varphi_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)}) is Hadamard differentiable at (μ,ν)(\mu,\nu), tangentially to ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu}.

Proof.

The argument follows the same strategy as Goldfeld et al. (2024, Thm. 3), so we only sketch the main steps and refer to that result for full details. For each i∈{0,1}i\in\{0,1\}, Goldfeld et al. (2024, Lem. 4) establish that the maps (μ,ν)↦φi(μ,ν)(\mu,\nu)\mapsto\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}, i∈{1,0}i\in\{1,0\}, are Hadamard differentiable in 𝒞​(𝒴)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y}). Since 𝒴\mathcal{Y} is compact, the canonical embedding 𝒞​(𝒴)↪L2​(𝒴)\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{Y})\hookrightarrow L^{2}(\mathcal{Y}) is continuous. It follows that, for every multi-index α=(α1,…,αd)∈ℕ0d\alpha=(\alpha_{1},\dots,\alpha_{d})\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d} (ℕ0=ℕ∪{0}\mathbb{N}_{0}=\mathbb{N}\cup\{0\}) with 0<|α|≤s0<\left|\alpha\right|\leq s, the functional (μ,ν)↦Dα​φi(μ,ν),𝒫μ×𝒫ν⊂ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→L2​(𝒴)(\mu,\nu)\mapsto D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)},\mathcal{P}_{\mu}\times\mathcal{P}_{\nu}\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to L^{2}(\mathcal{Y}) is Hadamard differentiable. We denote the derivative by [Dα​φi]′​[μ,ν]:ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν→L2​(P∗)[D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}]^{\prime}[\mu,\nu]:\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu}\to L^{2}(P^{*}).

Now consider paths (μt)t≥0=(μ+t​γt1)t≥0⊂𝒫μ(\mu_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(\mu+t\gamma_{t}^{1})_{t\geq 0}\subset\mathcal{P}_{\mu} and (νt)t≥0=(ν+t​γt2)t≥0⊂𝒫ν(\nu_{t})_{t\geq 0}=(\nu+t\gamma_{t}^{2})_{t\geq 0}\subset\mathcal{P}_{\nu} such that γti→γi\gamma_{t}^{i}\to\gamma^{i} as t↓0t\downarrow 0 in ℓ∞​(ℋ1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}). Pick any sequence tn↓0t_{n}\downarrow 0 as n→∞n\to\infty, then qtn:=tn−1​(φi(μtn,νtn)−φi(μ,ν))q_{t_{n}}:=t_{n}^{-1}\left(\varphi_{i}^{(\mu_{t_{n}},\nu_{t_{n}})}-\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}\right) is Cauchy in ℋ\mathcal{H}. This is because for any n,m∈ℕn,m\in\mathbb{N},

‖qtn−qtm‖ℋ2=∑|α|≤s‖Dα​φi(μtn,νtn)−Dα​φi(μ,ν)tn−Dα​φi(μtm,νtm)−Dα​φi(μ,ν)tm‖L2​(𝒴)2,\left\|q_{t_{n}}-q_{t_{m}}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}^{2}=\sum_{\left|\alpha\right|\leq s}\left\|\frac{D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu_{t_{n}},\nu_{t_{n}})}-D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}}{t_{n}}-\frac{D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu_{t_{m}},\nu_{t_{m}})}-D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}}{t_{m}}\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{Y})}^{2},

which converges to 0 because each component term in the finite sum of the RKHS above is Cauchy in L2L^{2}. Since there are finitely many terms for |α|≤s\left|\alpha\right|\leq s, the RHS converges to 0 as n,m→∞n,m\to\infty. By completeness of ℋ\mathcal{H}, the limit exists in ℋ\mathcal{H}. So let tn−1​(φi(μtn,νtn)−φi(μ,ν))→φi¯t_{n}^{-1}\left(\varphi_{i}^{(\mu_{t_{n}},\nu_{t_{n}})}-\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}\right)\to\overline{\varphi_{i}} in ℋ\mathcal{H}. Then, by definition of the limit in the Sobolev space ℋ\mathcal{H}, tn−1​(Dα​φi(μtn,νtn)−Dα​φi(μ,ν))→Dα​φ¯it_{n}^{-1}\left(D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu_{t_{n}},\nu_{t_{n}})}-D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}\right)\to D^{\alpha}\overline{\varphi}_{i} in L2​(𝒴)L^{2}(\mathcal{Y}). On the other hand, by the Hadamard differentiability of (μ,ν)↦Dα​φi(μ,ν)(\mu,\nu)\mapsto D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)}, the same limit must equal [Dα​φi]′​[μ,ν]​(γ1,γ2)[D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}]^{\prime}[\mu,\nu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}). Therefore,

Dα​φ¯i=[Dα​φi]′​[μ,ν]​(γ1,γ2)for all ​α∈ℕ0d​ with ​|α|≤s.D^{\alpha}\bar{\varphi}_{i}=[D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}]^{\prime}[\mu,\nu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})\qquad\text{for all }\alpha\in\mathbb{N}_{0}^{d}\text{ with }|\alpha|\leq s.

This shows that φ¯i\overline{\varphi}_{i} is exactly the Sobolev function in ℋ\mathcal{H} whose weak derivatives coincide with the coordinatewise directional derivatives, that is Dαφ¯i=[Dαφi]′[μ,ν])(γ1,γ2)D^{\alpha}\overline{\varphi}_{i}=[D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}]^{\prime}[\mu,\nu])(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}). Therefore, if the Hadamard derivative φi′​[μ,ν]\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu] exists, then φi′​[μ,ν]​(γ1,γ2)=φ¯i\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=\overline{\varphi}_{i}. Using this pointwise characterization, indeed the map (γ1,γ2)↦φi′​[μ,ν]​(γ1,γ2)(\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})\mapsto\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2}) is linear and continuous from ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu} into ℋ\mathcal{H} because Dα​φi′​[μ,ν]=[Dα​φi]′​[μ,ν]D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu]=[D^{\alpha}\varphi_{i}]^{\prime}[\mu,\nu] is a linear and continuous function on ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu} and summing over finitely such α\alpha gives the linearity and continuity of φi′​[μ,ν]\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu] on ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,ν\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\nu}. The explicit form of φi′​[μ,ν]\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\nu] is presented in Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Cor. 43). ∎

The following corollary provides the explicit form of the Hadamard derivatives of the centered entropic potentials maps υ1:(μ,ν)↦υ1(μ,ν)\upsilon_{1}:(\mu,\nu)\mapsto\upsilon_{1}^{(\mu,\nu)} and υ0:(μ,ν)↦υ0(μ,ν)\upsilon_{0}:(\mu,\nu)\mapsto\upsilon_{0}^{(\mu,\nu)} under the null.

Corollary C.7.

The Hadamard derivatives of υi:(μ,ν)↦υi(μ,ν),𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→ℋ\upsilon_{i}:(\mu,\nu)\mapsto\upsilon_{i}^{(\mu,\nu)},\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to\mathcal{H} for i∈{1,0}i\in\{1,0\} are given by

υ1′[μ,μ](γ1,γ2)=Kμ(γ1−γ2)+ερ𝟏and υ0′[μ,μ)](γ1,γ2)=−Kμ(γ1−γ2)−ερ𝟏\upsilon_{1}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=K_{\mu}(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2})+\varepsilon\rho\mathbf{1}\quad\textrm{and }\quad\upsilon_{0}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu)](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=-K_{\mu}(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2})-\varepsilon\rho\mathbf{1}

for a constant ρ∈ℝ\rho\in\mathbb{R}. This constant is fully expressed in Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Thm. 40), and omitted here because it is inconsequential in our case and ends up getting canceled out.

The corollary is stated without proof and follows directly from Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Cor. 43) by plugging υi′​[μ,μ]​(γ1,γ2)=φi′​[μ,μ]​(γ1,γ2)−φi′​[μ,μ]​(γ2−i,γ2−i)\upsilon_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})-\varphi_{i}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{2-i},\gamma^{2-i}) for i∈{1,0}i\in\{1,0\}.

Lemma C.8 (Thm. 48 in Kokot and Luedtke, 2025).

The map Sε:(μ,ν)↦Sε​(μ,ν),𝒫​(𝒴)×𝒫​(𝒴)⊂ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)→ℝS_{\varepsilon}:(\mu,\nu)\mapsto S_{\varepsilon}(\mu,\nu),\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\times\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y})\subset\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\to\mathbb{R} is Hadamard differentiable at (μ,μ)(\mu,\mu) with Hadamard derivative Sε′​[μ,μ]:ℳ0,μ×ℳ0,μ→ℝS_{\varepsilon}^{\prime}[\mu,\mu]:\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\times\mathcal{M}_{0,\mu}\to\mathbb{R} given by

Sε′′​[μ,μ]​(γ1,γ2)=(γ1−γ2)​Kμ​(γ1−γ2).S_{\varepsilon}^{\prime\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2})K_{\mu}(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2}).

We do not reproduce the full proof here, since the argument follows from Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Thm. 48) after replacing the required topologies. Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Thm. 48) derive the second-order Hadamard derivative (under the null) of a localized quadratic approximation of the Sinkhorn divergence from Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Lem. 45). In that argument, second-order Hadamard differentiability of the localized Sinkhorn divergence reduces to first-order Hadamard differentiability of the entropic potentials. This required first-order differentiability in the ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}) topology is established in Prop. C.6, together with an explicit characterization of the corresponding derivative. Substituting this derivative formula into the proof of Kokot and Luedtke (2025, Thm. 48) yields the stated Hadamard derivative Sε′′​[μ,μ]​(γ1,γ2)=(γ1−γ2)​Kμ​(γ1−γ2)S_{\varepsilon}^{\prime\prime}[\mu,\mu](\gamma^{1},\gamma^{2})=(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2})\,K_{\mu}\,(\gamma^{1}-\gamma^{2}).

Appendix D Pathwise Differentiability of STE

In this appendix, we prove the main results stated in Sec. 3. We begin by introducing notation that will be used throughout the proofs. For any score function s∈𝒫˙Ps\in\dot{\mathcal{P}}_{P}, define

sX​(x):=𝔼P​[s​(X,A,Y)|X=x]and sY|A,X​(y|a,x):=s​(x,a,y)−𝔼P​[s​(X,A,Y)|A=a,X=x].s_{X}(x):=\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[s(X,A,Y)\,|\,X=x\right]\quad\textrm{and }\quad s_{Y\,|\,A,X}(y\,|\,a,x):=s(x,a,y)-\mathbb{E}_{P}\left[s(X,A,Y)\,|\,A=a,X=x\right]. (32)

For notational convenience, we also introduce evaluation operators: for functions f:𝒵→ℝf:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, g:{0,1}×𝒳→ℝ,and ​h:𝒳→ℝg:\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R},\,\textrm{and }h:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} , we use the operator notation ℰz​f=f​(z)\mathscr{E}_{z}f=f(z), ℰa,x​g=g​(a,x)\mathscr{E}_{a,x}g=g(a,x), and ℰx​h=h​(x)\mathscr{E}_{x}h=h(x).

We recall the expectation operators PY|A,X,PA|X,and ​PXP_{Y\,|\,A,X},P_{A\,|\,X},\textrm{and }P_{X} introduced in (3). For f:𝒵→ℝf:\mathcal{Z}\to\mathbb{R}, a∈{0,1}a\in\{0,1\}, x∈𝒳x\in\mathcal{X}, and z′∈𝒵′z^{\prime}\in\mathcal{Z}^{\prime}, we define the shorthand notation

(PY|a,X​f)​(z′)\displaystyle(P_{Y\,|\,a,X}f)(z^{\prime}) :=(PY|A,X​f)​(x′,a,y′)\displaystyle:=(P_{Y\,|\,A,X}f)(x^{\prime},a,y^{\prime})
(PY|a,x​f)​(z′)\displaystyle(P_{Y\,|\,a,x}f)(z^{\prime}) :=(PY|A,X​f)​(x,a,y′)\displaystyle:=(P_{Y\,|\,A,X}f)(x,a,y^{\prime}) (33)

Since the right-hand side of the first equality is invariant in (a′,y′)(a^{\prime},y^{\prime}) and the second is invariant in z′z^{\prime}, we sometimes write PY|a,Xf)(x′):=(PY|a,Xf)(z′)P_{Y\,|\,a,X}f)(x^{\prime}):=(P_{Y\,|\,a,X}f)(z^{\prime}) for a generic (a′,y′)(a^{\prime},y^{\prime}) or PY|a,x​f:=(PY|a,x​f)​(z′)P_{Y\,|\,a,x}f:=(P_{Y\,|\,a,x}f)(z^{\prime}) for a generic z′z^{\prime}. We also define the composed operators

PA,X:=PX​PA|XandPY,A|X:=PA|X​PY|A,X.P_{A,X}:=P_{X}P_{A\,|\,X}\quad\text{and}\quad P_{Y,A\,|\,X}:=P_{A\,|\,X}P_{Y\,|\,A,X}. (34)

Specifically, for f:{0,1}×𝒳→ℝf:\{0,1\}\times\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R} and g:𝒳→ℝg:\mathcal{X}\to\mathbb{R}, we set PA|X​f​(x)=∑a∈{1,0}f​(a,x)​eP​(a|x)P_{A\,|\,X}f(x)=\sum_{a\in\{1,0\}}f(a,x)\,e_{P}(a\,|\,x), PA,X​f​(x)=∫𝒳∑a∈{1,0}f​(a,x)​eP​(a|x)​d​PX​(x)P_{A,X}f(x)=\int_{\mathcal{X}}\sum_{a\in\{1,0\}}f(a,x)\,e_{P}(a\,|\,x)\,dP_{X}(x), and PX​g=∫𝒳g​(x)​𝑑PX​(x)P_{X}g=\int_{\mathcal{X}}g(x)\,dP_{X}(x).

D.1 First-order pathwise differentiability of STE

The first-order pathwise differentiability of 𝒮=Sε∘J∘Ψ\mathscr{S}=S_{\varepsilon}\circ J\circ\Psi is established in three steps: (1) Hadamard differentiability of SεS_{\varepsilon} (Lem. C.4), (2) Hadamard differentiability of JJ (Lem. D.1), and (3) pathwise differentiability of Ψ\Psi (Lem. D.2).

Lemma D.1 (Hadamard derivative of JJ).

The functional J:ℋ×ℋ→ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)J:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H}\to\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}) is Hadamard differentiable at every (f,g)∈ℋ×ℋ(f,g)\in\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} and the Hadamard derivative J′​[f,g]:ℋ×ℋ→ℓ∞​(ℋ1)×ℓ∞​(ℋ1)J^{\prime}[f,g]:\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H}\to\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})\times\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1}) is given by

J′​[f,g]​(h1,h2)=J​(h1,h2).J^{\prime}[f,g](h^{1},h^{2})=J(h^{1},h^{2}).
Proof.

Consider paths (ft)t>0(f_{t})_{t>0} and (gt)t>0(g_{t})_{t>0} in ℋ\mathcal{H} such that ft=f+t​ht1f_{t}=f+th_{t}^{1} and gt=g+t​ht2g_{t}=g+th_{t}^{2} such that ht1→h1h_{t}^{1}\to h^{1} and ht2→h2h_{t}^{2}\to h^{2} as t→0t\to 0 in ℋ\mathcal{H} for some (h1,h2)∈ℋ×ℋ(h^{1},h^{2})\in\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H}. Then,

1t​[J​(ft,gt)−J​(f,g)]\displaystyle\frac{1}{t}\left[J(f_{t},g_{t})-J(f,g)\right] =J​(ht1,ht2)\displaystyle=J(h_{t}^{1},h_{t}^{2})
⟹limt→01t​[J​(ft,gt)−J​(f,g)]\displaystyle\implies\lim_{t\to 0}\frac{1}{t}\left[J(f_{t},g_{t})-J(f,g)\right] =limt→0J​(ht1,ht2).\displaystyle=\lim_{t\to 0}J(h_{t}^{1},h_{t}^{2}).

We have that J​(ht1,ht2)J(h_{t}^{1},h_{t}^{2}) converges to J​(h1,h2)J(h^{1},h^{2}) in the supnorm as

‖J​(ht1,ht2)−J​(h1,h2)‖ℓ∞​(ℋ1)\displaystyle\left\|J(h_{t}^{1},h_{t}^{2})-J(h^{1},h^{2})\right\|_{\ell^{\infty}(\mathcal{H}_{1})} =suph∈ℋ1|⟨h,ht1−h1⟩ℋ|+suph∈ℋ1|⟨h,ht2−h2⟩ℋ|\displaystyle=\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{1}}\left|\left\langle h,h_{t}^{1}-h^{1}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\right|+\sup_{h\in\mathcal{H}_{1}}\left|\left\langle h,h_{t}^{2}-h^{2}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}\right|
≤‖ht1−h1‖ℋ+‖ht2−h2‖ℋ→0.\displaystyle\leq\left\|h_{t}^{1}-h^{1}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}+\left\|h_{t}^{2}-h^{2}\right\|_{\mathcal{H}}\to 0.

This completes the proof. ∎

Lemma D.2 (Pathwise derivative of Ψ\Psi Luedtke and Chung, 2024, Ex. 3).

Recall that (1) the Sobolev kernel k:𝒴×𝒴→ℝk:\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{Y}\to\mathbb{R} is bounded, symmetric, and positive definite and (2) the model 𝒫\mathcal{P} satisfies strong positivity. Then, the parameter Ψ:𝒫→ℋ×ℋ\Psi:\mathcal{P}\to\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} is pathwise differentiable at all P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} with local parameter D​ΨP:𝒫˙P→ℋ×ℋD\Psi_{P}:\dot{\mathcal{P}}_{P}\to\mathcal{H}\times\mathcal{H} given by

D​ΨP​(s)=[D​ψP1​(s)D​ψP0​(s)]=[∫𝒳∫𝒴k​(y,⋅)​[sY|A,X​(y| 1,x)+sX​(x)]​PY|A,X​(d​y| 1,x)​PX​(d​x)∫𝒳∫𝒴k​(y,⋅)​[sY|A,X​(y| 0,x)+sX​(x)]​PY|A,X​(d​y| 0,x)​PX​(d​x)].D\Psi_{P}(s)=\begin{bmatrix}D{\psi}^{1}_{P}(s)\\ D{\psi}^{0}_{P}(s)\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}\int_{\mathcal{X}}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}k(y,\cdot)\left[s_{Y\,|\,A,X}(y\,|\,1,x)+s_{X}(x)\right]\,P_{Y\,|\,A,X}(dy\,|\,1,x)\,P_{X}(dx)\\ \int_{\mathcal{X}}\int_{\mathcal{Y}}k(y,\cdot)\left[s_{Y\,|\,A,X}(y\,|\,0,x)+s_{X}(x)\right]\,P_{Y\,|\,A,X}(dy\,|\,0,x)\,P_{X}(dx)\end{bmatrix}. (35)

Finally, we combine three ingredients through a chain rule: the Hadamard differentiability of the Sinkhorn divergence SεS_{\varepsilon}, the Hadamard differentiability of the canonical embedding JJ, and the pathwise differentiability of KME Ψ\Psi. Together, these results yield the local parameter of the STE.

D.2 Second-order pathwise differentiability of STE under the null

Appendix E One-Step Estimators of STE

Let P^\widehat{P} be an initial estimator of P∗P^{*} constructed from nn independent samples drawn from P∗P^{*}, and let PnP_{n} denote the empirical measure based on another set of nn independent samples from P∗P^{*}, taken independently of P^\widehat{P}. In this section, we study the asymptotic distributions of the one-step estimator for STE under the alternative hypothesis (P1∗≠P0∗)(P_{1}^{*}\neq P_{0}^{*}), and of the second-order one-step estimator for STE under the null hypothesis (P1∗=P0∗)(P_{1}^{*}=P_{0}^{*}). Throughout this section, for notational convenience, we write υ^a\widehat{\upsilon}_{a} for υa(P^1,P^0)\upsilon_{a}^{(\widehat{P}_{1},\widehat{P}_{0})}, υa∗\upsilon_{a}^{*} for υa(P1∗,P0∗)\upsilon_{a}^{(P_{1}^{*},P_{0}^{*})}, e^​(a∣x)\hat{e}(a\mid x) for eP^​(a∣x)e_{\widehat{P}}(a\mid x), and e∗​(a∣x)e^{*}(a\mid x) for eP∗​(a∣x)e_{P^{*}}(a\mid x), for a∈{1,0}a\in\{1,0\}.

E.1 Limit theorem for first-order one-step estimator

As discussed in Sec. 4, the one-step estimator 𝒮^=𝒮​(P^)+Pn​𝒮˙P^\widehat{\mathscr{S}}=\mathscr{S}(\widehat{P})+P_{n}\dot{\mathscr{S}}_{\widehat{P}} can be expanded as

Appendix F One-Step Estimator of MMD Distribution Treatment Effect

As a benchmark, we also compute first- and second-order one-step estimators for the maximum mean discrepancy between counterfactual outcome distributions; we call this the MMD treatment effect (MTE). The corresponding EIFs are derived using the same framework as for the Sinkhorn divergence; however, smoothness with respect to the underlying kernel mean embeddings is immediate for MMD due to its quadratic form.

The (squared) MMD functional is defined as

ℳ:P∈𝒫↦12MMD2(ψ1(P)),ψ0(P))=12∥ψ1(P))−ψ0(P))∥2𝒢,\mathscr{M}:P\in\mathcal{P}\mapsto\frac{1}{2}\text{MMD}^{2}\left(\psi^{1}(P)),\,\psi^{0}(P)\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left\|\psi^{1}(P))-\psi^{0}(P))\right\|^{2}_{\mathcal{G}}, (38)

where recall that 𝒢\mathcal{G} is the Gaussian RKHS with kernel gε​(y1,y2)=exp⁡(−‖y1−y2‖2/2​ε)g_{\varepsilon}(y_{1},y_{2})=\exp(-\|y_{1}-y_{2}\|^{2}/2\varepsilon) and KME operator 𝔤​(μ)=∫gε​(⋅,y)​𝑑μ​(y)\mathfrak{g}(\mu)=\int g_{\varepsilon}(\cdot,y)d\mu(y).

Lemma F.1 (MMD first-order local parameter, Ex. 3 in Luedtke and Chung (2024)).

The parameter ℳ:𝒫→ℝ\mathscr{M}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{R} is pathwise differentiable at P∈𝒫P\in\mathcal{P} with first-order EIF given by

ℳ˙P=(I−(I−(I−PX)​PA|X)​PY|A,X)​f,\dot{\mathscr{M}}_{P}=(I-(I-(I-P_{X})P_{A\,|\,X})P_{Y\,|\,A,X})f,

where f​(x,a,y)=2​a−1eP​(a|x)​(𝔤​(P1)​(y)−𝔤​(P0)​(y))f(x,a,y)=\frac{2a-1}{e_{P}(a\,|\,x)}\left(\mathfrak{g}(P_{1})(y)-\mathfrak{g}(P_{0})(y)\right).

Proof.

This lemma follows by applying the automatic differentiation algorithm in Thm. 1 of Luedtke (2026) with the composition of two primitives from that work: the kernel mean embedding in Lem. S11 in Appx. C.2.5 and the squared (RKHS) norm in Appx. C.4.3. ∎

Lemma F.2 (MMD second-order local parameter).

The parameter ℳ:𝒫→ℝ\mathscr{M}:\mathcal{P}\to\mathbb{R} is second- order pathwise differentiable at all P∈ℋ0P\in\mathscr{H}_{0} with second- order EIF, denoted by ℳ¨P∈L2​(P⊗2)\ddot{\mathscr{M}}_{P}\in L^{2}(P^{\otimes 2}), and equal to

Lem. F.1 and Lem. F.2 yield the first and second order EIF used to construct the one-step estimator of ℳ​(P∗)\mathscr{M}(P^{*}) and the test statistic for testing the null hypothesis. The one-step estimator of ℳ​(P∗)\mathscr{M}(P^{*}) is

Finite sample implementation.

From a computational perspective, the first-order EIF of MMD is obtained by applying Alg. 1 with 𝐔1=𝐆​(𝐏1−𝐏0)\mathbf{U}^{1}=\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{P}^{1}-\mathbf{P}^{0}) and 𝐔2=−𝐆​(𝐏1−𝐏0)\mathbf{U}^{2}=-\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{P}^{1}-\mathbf{P}^{0}). The second-order EIF is computed via Alg. 2 by omitting the intermediate operator application (Step 3) and replacing 𝐊\mathbf{K} with 𝐆\mathbf{G} in Step 4.

Appendix G Algorithms for Finite-Sample Implementation

Here we present the algorithms for debiasing the STE estimator using first-order EIF computations in Alg. 1 and second-order EIF computations in Alg. 2. Refer to the precomputations in Sec. 5.

Since qn,ε→𝑝qεq_{n,\varepsilon}\xrightarrow{p}q_{\varepsilon} with qε>0q_{\varepsilon}>0, we have that qn,ε=Op​(1)q_{n,\varepsilon}=O_{p}(1) and 1qn,ε=Op​(1)\frac{1}{q_{n,\varepsilon}}=O_{p}(1) for each ε∈Ξ\varepsilon\in\Xi. It follows that 𝒯n,εqn,ε→𝑝∞\frac{\mathcal{T}_{n,\varepsilon}}{q_{n,\varepsilon}}\xrightarrow{p}\infty for all ε∈Ξ\varepsilon\in\Xi. Hence,

𝒯nagg=maxε∈Ξ⁡𝒯n,εqn,ε≥𝒯n,ε1qn,ε1→𝑃∞.\mathcal{T}_{n}^{\mathrm{agg}}=\max_{\varepsilon\in\Xi}\frac{\mathcal{T}_{n,\varepsilon}}{q_{n,\varepsilon}}\geq\frac{\mathcal{T}_{n,\varepsilon_{1}}}{q_{n,\varepsilon_{1}}}\xrightarrow{P}\infty.

Finally, because Ξ\Xi is finite and each W​(ε)/qεW(\varepsilon)/q_{\varepsilon} is tight, the random variable WaggW^{\textrm{agg}} has finite (1−α)(1-\alpha)-quantile. Therefore,

Pr⁡(𝒯nagg>q1−α​(Wagg))→1,\Pr\!\left(\mathcal{T}_{n}^{\mathrm{agg}}>q_{1-\alpha}(W^{\mathrm{agg}})\right)\to 1,

so the proposed test rejects with probability tending to 11. ∎

Appendix I Experimental Details

For our experiments, we use a sample splitting approach in which an effective sample of size 2​n2n is divided evenly. The first nn observations are used to construct an initial estimator P^\widehat{P} of P∗P^{*}, and the remaining nn observations are used to form the empirical distribution PnP_{n}.

I.1 Datasets

I.1.1 Simulations.

The covariates X∼𝒩​(𝟎3,I3)X\sim\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{0}_{3},I_{3}), and the treatment assignment model is logistic such that,

A|X=x∼Bernoulli(expit(𝟏3⊤x))).A\,|\,X=x\sim\text{Bernoulli}(\text{expit}(\mathbf{1}_{3}^{\top}x))).

Throughout Exp (i) and (ii), we maintain a fixed covariance matrix Σ\Sigma. For Exp (i) (mean difference), the outcome YY given (A,X)(A,X) is sampled as

Y|(A=a,X=x)∼{𝒩​(𝟎2,Σ)if ​a=0,𝒩​(θ​𝟏2,Σ)if ​a=1.,Y\,|\,(A=a,X=x)\sim\begin{cases}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{0}_{2},\,\Sigma})&\quad\text{if }a=0,\\ \mathcal{N}({\theta\mathbf{1}_{2},\,\Sigma})&\quad\text{if }a=1.\end{cases},

For Exp (ii) (covariance difference), the outcome YY given (A,X)(A,X) is sampled as

Y|(A=a,X=x)∼{𝒩​(𝟎2,Σ)if ​a=0,𝒩​(𝟎2,Σ+θ​(u​v⊤+v​u⊤))if ​a=1,Y\,|\,(A=a,X=x)\sim\begin{cases}\mathcal{N}({\mathbf{0}_{2},\,\Sigma})&\quad\text{if }a=0,\\ \mathcal{N}({\mathbf{0}_{2},\,\Sigma+\theta(uv^{\top}+vu^{\top})})&\quad\text{if }a=1,\end{cases}

where uu and vv are the eigenvectors of Σ\Sigma. Figure 3 illustrates the resulting 95%95\% ellipsoids for varying θ\theta.

Simulations for aggregated test.

We replicate the simulation setup of Exp (ii), but now evaluate the tests over a grid of ε\varepsilon values of the form ε=η​m\varepsilon=\eta m, where mm is the median heuristic and η∈{0.25,0.5,1,2,4}\eta\in\{0.25,0.5,1,2,4\}. For each fixed ε\varepsilon, we compute the corresponding MTE- and STE-based test statistics and p-values, and we additionally evaluate the aggregated procedures MTEAgg and STEAgg. The results are shown in Fig. 4 under both the null (Exp (ii) with θ=0.0\theta=0.0) and an alternative (Exp (ii) with θ=0.8\theta=0.8). Under the null, both MTE- and STE-based tests exhibit lower type-I error as ε\varepsilon increases. Under the alternative, for STE, power initially improves with ε\varepsilon, but eventually deteriorates when ε\varepsilon becomes too large, reflecting oversmoothing and a loss of sensitivity to distributional differences; in this regime, Sinkhorn divergence begins to behave more like MMD (Feydy et al., 2019). Interestingly, for STE power is also lower when ε\varepsilon is too small, which is consistent with the numerical instability of Sinkhorn iterations at low regularization. Overall, this experiment recovers the expected bias-variance tradeoff in the choice of ε\varepsilon for STE. Among the values considered, the strongest performance is attained near the median heuristic, which we therefore recommend as a practical default.

I.1.2 PCam Dataset

We provide here the exact data-generating mechanism used for the image-outcome experiments. For each unit, covariates are generated as X∼𝒩​(0,I5)X\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{5}). Conditional on X=xX=x, a latent disease status S∈{0,1}S\in\{0,1\} is sampled from a Bernoulli distribution with success probability expit​(π0+π1⊤​x)\mathrm{expit}(\pi_{0}+\pi_{1}^{\top}x), where S=1S=1 denotes metastatic tissue. Treatment assignment A∈{0,1}A\in\{0,1\} is generated independently given X=xX=x from a Bernoulli distribution with success probability expit​(γ0+γ1⊤​x)\mathrm{expit}(\gamma_{0}+\gamma_{1}^{\top}x), inducing confounding through shared dependence on XX.

Outcome images YY are sampled from the empirical PCam image distributions conditional on (S,A,X)(S,A,X). Specifically, if S=0S=0, outcomes are drawn from the empirical distribution supported on 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0}. If S=1S=1 and A=0A=0, outcomes are drawn from 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1}. If S=1S=1 and A=1A=1, outcomes are drawn from 𝒟0\mathcal{D}_{0} with probability q​(x)=expit​(β0+β1⊤​x)q(x)=\mathrm{expit}(\beta_{0}+\beta_{1}^{\top}x) and from 𝒟1\mathcal{D}_{1} otherwise. This construction induces heterogeneous, covariate-dependent treatment effects on the counterfactual distributions while preserving overlap and positivity.

I.2 Compute details

The code was written in Python 3 and we use PyTorch for automatic differentiation. All our experiments were conducted on a CUDA-enabled machine with 12GB GPU memory, 64GB RAM, and 24 vCPUs. Although the experiments were run on a GPU, we observe similar complexity trends for CPU implementations. Fig. 6 plots the average wall-clock time (averaged over 20 Monte Carlo simulations) and memory usage across increasing sample sizes nn for both GPU and CPU implementations.

I.3 Acceleration recommendations

We now make the computational bottlenecks of the second-order one-step STE estimator explicit and summarize practical acceleration strategies. From Sec. 5, the total computational complexity is O​(n2​(n+t))O(n^{2}(n+t)), where nn is the sample size and tt is the number of Sinkhorn iterations. This cost is driven primarily by the Sinkhorn algorithm, which contributes O​(n2​t)O(n^{2}t), and Algorithm 2, which contributes O​(n3)O(n^{3}). In addition, once the Gram matrix of the second-order EIF has been formed, the second-order bias-correction term requires a U-statistic computation, which incurs an additional quadratic computational load. We now discuss standard acceleration techniques that can be incorporated directly into our framework. While we expect these strategies to yield empirical gains similar to those reported in the existing literature, a full asymptotic analysis of the resulting accelerated procedures is beyond the scope of the present paper.

Sinkhorn algorithm.

To accelerate the Sinkhorn step, several complementary strategies are available. Greenkhorn (Altschuler et al., 2017) replaces full alternating row/column normalizations by greedy coordinate updates, which often improves practical performance while retaining the same dense-kernel representation. Batch Greenkhorn methods (Kostic et al., 2022) extend this idea by updating batches of coordinates and provide refined convergence guarantees. These approaches aim to reduce the amount of scaling work required for convergence, but they do not by themselves eliminate the O​(n2)O(n^{2}) cost of storing and multiplying by a dense Gibbs kernel. To address this bottleneck, Nyström-Sinkhorn (Altschuler et al., 2019) approximates the Gibbs kernel Ki​j=e−Ci​j/εK_{ij}=e^{-C_{ij}/\varepsilon} using a low-rank Nyström factorization, reducing per-iteration kernel-vector multiplication costs and memory usage from O​(n2)O(n^{2}) to O​(n​r)O(nr), where rr is the approximation rank. These approaches can be incorporated into our one-step STE estimator to reduce the per-iteration computational cost.

Algorithm 2 acceleration.

A natural way to reduce the O​(n3)O(n^{3}) cost of Alg. 2 is to replace the dense discretized self-transport kernel 𝐗\mathbf{X}, defined in line 3 by

𝐗i​j=exp⁡{𝐅i+𝐅j−𝐆i​jε},\mathbf{X}_{ij}=\exp\!\left\{\frac{\mathbf{F}_{i}+\mathbf{F}_{j}-\mathbf{G}_{ij}}{\varepsilon}\right\},

with a rank-rr Nyström approximation 𝐗~=C​W†​C⊤=U​V⊤\tilde{\mathbf{X}}=CW^{\dagger}C^{\top}=UV^{\top} with r≪nr\ll n. This is well aligned with prior work on scalable entropic OT, where low-rank Nyström approximations are used to compress the Gibbs kernel while preserving the Sinkhorn scaling structure (Altschuler et al., 2019). In our setting, the cubic bottleneck arises because line 5 requires solving a dense n×nn\times n linear system,

𝐌=(I−(𝐏1⊙𝐗)2)−1​(𝐗−𝟏𝟏⊤/n),\mathbf{M}=\bigl(I-(\mathbf{P}^{1}\odot\mathbf{X})^{2}\bigr)^{-1}\left(\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top}/n\right),

and because the subsequent contractions 𝐏𝐌\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M} in lines 8-10 amount to repeated dense matrix multiplications, each of overall order n3n^{3}. Replacing 𝐗\mathbf{X} by 𝐗~\tilde{\mathbf{X}} lowers both costs: first, if A:=𝐏1⊙𝐗~A:=\mathbf{P}^{1}\odot\tilde{\mathbf{X}} is represented in low-rank form as A=U~​V⊤A=\tilde{U}V^{\top}, then

A2=(U~​V⊤)​(U~​V⊤)=U~​B​V⊤,B:=V⊤​U~∈ℝr×r,A^{2}=(\tilde{U}V^{\top})(\tilde{U}V^{\top})=\tilde{U}BV^{\top},\qquad B:=V^{\top}\tilde{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{r\times r},

so (I−A2)−1\bigl(I-A^{2}\bigr)^{-1} can be applied via the Woodbury identity using only an r×rr\times r inner solve, reducing line 5 from O​(n3)O(n^{3}) to O​(n​r2+r3)O(nr^{2}+r^{3}) after the low-rank factors are formed. Second, every multiplication by an n×nn\times n matrix generated from 𝐗\mathbf{X} can be evaluated through the factorization U​V⊤UV^{\top}, costing O​(n​r)O(nr) per vector and O​(n2​r)O(n^{2}r) per matrix block, so the contractions 𝐏𝐌\mathbf{P}\mathbf{M} drop from O​(n3)O(n^{3}) to O​(n2​r)O(n^{2}r). The remaining operations in the algorithm: forming 𝐗\mathbf{X}, applying 𝐃A,X\mathbf{\mathbf{D}}_{A,X}, and elementwise products are at most quadratic, so under a Nyström representation the total complexity of the second-order routine is reduced from O​(n3)O(n^{3}) to roughly O​(n2​r+n​r2+r3)O(n^{2}r+nr^{2}+r^{3}), with memory reduced from O​(n2)O(n^{2}) to O​(n​r)O(nr). Therefore, a Nyström approximation to the discretized Sinkhorn self-transport kernel is a direct and computationally efficient way to scale the second-order correction while retaining the kernel structure induced by the entropic potentials.

UU-statistic computation.

The O​(n2)O(n^{2}) complexity of the U-statistic, standard in kernel two-sample testing, can be mitigated using linear-time approximations (Gretton et al., 2012) or incomplete U-statistics (Schrab et al., 2022). Both can be directly substituted into the second-order bias-correction term of the STE one-step estimator.
